facts.text: On January 1, 1835, the U.S. owed just $33,733, the only time the government has paid off its interest-bearing debt.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Historical Debt Outstanding
facts.note: Fiscal Data record 1835-01-01 = $33,733.05; TreasuryDirect says all interest-bearing debt was paid off by January 1835, the only time.

facts.text: As of October 2026, the national debt grows about $6.6 billion a day, or roughly $76,000 every second.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny

facts.text: Charlie Chaplin, Mary Pickford and Douglas Fairbanks toured the country holding rallies to sell Liberty Bonds in World War I.
facts.source: Federal Reserve History, Liberty Bonds

facts.text: Japan is the largest foreign holder of U.S. Treasuries, with $1.104 trillion as of July 2026.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury, Treasury International Capital Table 5: Major Foreign Holders of Treasury Securities (July 2026)

facts.text: A June 20, 1790 dinner hosted by Jefferson traded Hamilton's plan to assume state war debts for a capital on the Potomac.
facts.source: National Archives, Prologue blog: The Compromise of 1790
facts.note: Prologue: Madison agreed not to block debt assumption; Congress passed the Residence Act in July 1790 and the Funding Act in August 1790.

facts.text: From 1940 to 1945, World War II multiplied the national debt sixfold, from $43 billion to $259 billion.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Historical Debt Outstanding

facts.text: On August 18, 2026, the national debt passed $40 trillion for the first time.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny
facts.note: First record at or above $40T is 2026-08-18 ($40.047T).

facts.text: The U.S. paid for the Louisiana Purchase with $11.25 million in 6 percent bonds plus $3.75 million in claims it took on.
facts.source: American Heritage, We Banked Them
facts.note: American Heritage: Barings turned title over to the U.S. in exchange for $11,250,000 in 6 percent bonds; the remaining $3,750,000 covered private American claims against France.

facts.text: In fiscal 2026, net interest on the debt topped $1 trillion for the first time, reaching $1.05 trillion.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Monthly Treasury Statement Table 9 (September 2026)
facts.note: MTS Table 9: Net Interest FY2026 = $1,051.8B; FY2025 = $970.4B. Earlier years were lower.

facts.text: The Second Liberty Bond Act of September 24, 1917 created the first overall cap on federal debt, the root of today's debt limit.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service RL31967, The Debt Limit: History and Recent Increases
facts.note: CRS RL31967 summary and IF10292: the aggregate debt limit was first created in 1917.

facts.text: In 1935, the Treasury introduced the 'baby bond': pay $18.75 now for a savings bond with a $25 face value.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of U.S. Savings Bonds (timeline)

facts.text: As of October 2026, the national debt works out to about $117,600 for every U.S. resident.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny
facts.note: Debt $40.329T (2026-10-14) divided by U.S. population 343.0 million (Census-based FRED POPTHM, Aug 2026).

facts.text: The Civil War grew the debt more than 4,000 percent, from $65 million in 1860 to about $2.7 billion in 1865.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Understanding the National Debt
facts.note: Fiscal Data: debt grew over 4,000 percent from $65 million in 1860. Historical Debt Outstanding: 1860 = $64.8 million, 1865 = $2.68 billion.

facts.text: John Adams signed a five million guilder loan with Amsterdam bankers on June 11, 1782 to fund the young nation.
facts.source: Massachusetts Historical Society, Papers of John Adams, vol. 13
facts.note: Contract for 5 million guilders at 5 percent with three Amsterdam firms.

facts.text: Moody's cut the U.S. from Aaa to Aa1 on May 16, 2025, the last of the big three agencies to drop its top rating.
facts.source: Moody's, 2025 United States Sovereign Rating Action
facts.note: S&P cut the U.S. to AA+ on August 5, 2011; Fitch on August 1, 2023; Moody's on May 16, 2025. PGPF reports no 2026 rating action.

facts.text: New York's National Debt Clock was retired on September 7, 2000, as budget surpluses paid down the debt.
facts.source: White House archives, Statement by the President: National Debt Clock (Sept 7, 2000)

facts.text: After the July 2025 debt-limit increase, the debt climbed from $37 trillion to $38 trillion in just 71 days.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny
facts.note: $37T first reached 2025-08-11; $38T first reached 2025-10-21 (71 days).

facts.text: Treasury Secretary Albert Gallatin cut the debt to $45.2 million by 1812, then the War of 1812 nearly tripled it.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt
facts.note: Fiscal Data Historical Debt Outstanding: 1812-01-01 = $45.2 million; 1816-01-01 = $127.3 million (2.8 times). TreasuryDirect credits Gallatin with the paydown.

facts.text: Franklin Roosevelt bought the first Series E war bond himself, on May 1, 1941, from Treasury Secretary Henry Morgenthau.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of U.S. Savings Bonds (timeline)
facts.note: Timeline: Series E announced April 30, 1941; on sale the next day, when Roosevelt bought the first one from Morgenthau.

facts.text: CBO projects debt held by the public will hit a record 108 percent of GDP by 2030, passing the 106 percent peak of 1946.
facts.source: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, on CBO's 2026 long-term outlook
facts.note: CRFB on CBO extended baseline: 108 percent in 2030, described as a record; CBO February 2026 outlook cites the previous high of 106 percent in 1946.

facts.text: In 1835, the federal budget surplus of $17.9 million was bigger than total government spending that year.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: Americans still hold $146 billion in U.S. savings securities, as of September 30, 2026.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Monthly Statement of the Public Debt Table 1 (September 2026)
facts.note: MSPD Table 1: United States Savings Securities = $146,290 million.

facts.text: Between 1916 and 1919, World War I multiplied the national debt more than seven times, from $3.6 billion to over $25 billion.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Historical Debt Outstanding
facts.note: Fiscal Data: 1916-07-01 = $3.61 billion. TreasuryDirect and CRS RL31967: total debt exceeded $25 billion (about $25.5 billion) at the end of FY1919. 25.5 / 3.6 = 7.1.

facts.text: Before World War I, Congress often approved federal borrowing one project at a time, such as the Panama Canal.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service RL31967, The Debt Limit: History and Recent Increases

facts.text: In fiscal 2026, net interest on the debt ($1.05 trillion) cost more than national defense ($965 billion).
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Monthly Treasury Statement Table 9 (September 2026)
facts.note: Net Interest $1,051.8B; National Defense $965.2B (FYTD through September 2026).

facts.text: During the 1930s, the national debt more than doubled, from $16.2 billion in 1930 to $40.4 billion in 1939.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Historical Debt Outstanding

facts.text: The national debt has doubled in a decade, from $19.7 trillion in October 2016 to $40.3 trillion in October 2026.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny

facts.text: Norman Rockwell's Four Freedoms paintings toured department stores in 1943 and helped sell $130 million in war bonds.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of U.S. Savings Bonds (timeline)

facts.text: Treasury's records put the debt at exactly $75,463,476.52 on January 1, 1791, counted down to the penny.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Historical Debt Outstanding

facts.text: Foreign investors held $9.25 trillion of U.S. Treasuries in July 2026, by Treasury's international capital data.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury, Treasury International Capital Table 5: Major Foreign Holders of Treasury Securities (July 2026)

facts.text: In fiscal 2020, the pandemic added $4.2 trillion to the debt, taking it from $22.7 trillion to $26.9 trillion.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Historical Debt Outstanding
facts.note: 2019-09-30 = $22.72 trillion; 2020-09-30 = $26.95 trillion; difference $4.23 trillion.

facts.text: Fitch cut the U.S. from AAA to AA+ on August 1, 2023, citing falling governance standards and a rising debt burden.
facts.source: Peter G. Peterson Foundation, With $40 Trillion in Debt, Is the U.S. Headed for More Credit Downgrades?
facts.note: Date and 'steady deterioration in standards of governance' language from Reuters-sourced coverage (The Week, Aug 2, 2023); PGPF page notes Fitch cited high and rising debt.

facts.text: About 20 million Americans bought Liberty Bonds in World War I, in a country of only 24 million households.
facts.source: Federal Reserve History, Liberty Bonds

facts.text: In July 1939, Congress set the first overall debt limit at $45 billion, only about 10 percent above the $40.4 billion debt.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service RL31967, The Debt Limit: History and Recent Increases

facts.text: In fiscal 2026, the government paid about $33,000 in net interest every second.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Monthly Treasury Statement Table 9 (September 2026)
facts.note: $1,051.8B divided by 31,536,000 seconds = $33,350 per second.

facts.text: In 1943, schoolchildren's bond and stamp purchases paid for 90,000 Jeeps under the Schools at War program.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of U.S. Savings Bonds (timeline)

facts.text: It took 12.6 years for the debt to go from $5 to $10 trillion, 8.9 years to reach $20 trillion, and 4.4 more to hit $30 trillion.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny

facts.text: CBO projects net interest will more than double from $970 billion in 2025 to $2.1 trillion in 2036.
facts.source: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, on CBO's February 2026 Budget and Economic Outlook

facts.text: Alexander Hamilton wrote that a national debt, if it is not excessive, will be to us a national blessing.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: Debt held by the public reached about 100 percent of GDP in fiscal 2026, a share topped only in 1945 and 1946.
facts.source: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, FY 2026 deficit estimate (Oct 1, 2026)

facts.text: After World War II, Congress cut the debt limit from $300 billion to $275 billion and left it there until 1954.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service RL31967, The Debt Limit: History and Recent Increases

facts.text: The first Liberty Loan opened on April 28, 1917, just 22 days after the U.S. declared war in World War I.
facts.source: Federal Reserve History, Liberty Bonds

facts.text: In July 2026, the United Kingdom held a record $998 billion of U.S. Treasuries, second only to Japan.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury, Treasury International Capital Table 5: Major Foreign Holders of Treasury Securities (July 2026)
facts.note: TIC Table 5: UK $998.3B in July 2026; the series high in the Treasury history file (through 2025) is $901.3B. Treasury cautions custody data can misattribute owners.

facts.text: In 2008, New York's debt clock ran out of digits when the national debt passed $10 trillion.
facts.source: NBC News, National-Debt Clock Maxed Out (Oct 2008)
facts.note: Debt to the Penny: first record above $10 trillion is 2008-09-30 ($10.025T).

facts.text: As of October 2026, the national debt equals roughly $299,000 for every U.S. household.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny
facts.note: Debt $40.329T (2026-10-14) divided by 134.79 million households (Census Current Population Survey via FRED TTLHH, 2025).

facts.text: Einstein hand-copied his 1905 relativity paper in 1943 to help sell war bonds; it now sits in the Library of Congress.
facts.source: Library of Congress, Albert Einstein Papers finding aid
facts.note: Finding aid: autographed fair copy of the 1905 paper made by Einstein in 1943 and donated to promote the sale of war bonds.

facts.text: Debt held by the public peaked at 106 percent of GDP in 1946, then fell to 22 percent by 1974.
facts.source: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis: Federal Debt Held by the Public as Percent of GDP
facts.note: FRED FYPUGDA188S: 1946 = 106.31 percent (series maximum); 1974 = 22.24 percent. Dollar debt kept rising; the share of GDP fell.

facts.text: On September 30, 2026, the average rate on all U.S. debt was 3.53 percent, while the 10-year yield was 5.29 percent.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Average Interest Rates on Treasury Securities (September 2026)
facts.note: Average rate on total interest-bearing debt = 3.531 percent. 10-year par yield on 2026-09-30 = 5.29 percent (Treasury Daily Par Yield Curve Rates).

facts.text: The 1862 Legal Tender Act authorized $150 million in U.S. notes and $500 million in bonds to pay for the Civil War.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: CBO's long-term outlook has debt held by the public reaching 175 percent of GDP, about $168 trillion, by 2056.
facts.source: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, on CBO's 2026 long-term outlook

facts.text: After peaking at $2.77 billion in 1866, the debt fell 44 percent over 27 years, to $1.55 billion in 1893.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Historical Debt Outstanding
facts.note: 1866-07-01 = $2.773 billion; 1893-07-01 = $1.546 billion; decline 44 percent.

facts.text: A World War I bond poster slogan read, 'If you can't enlist, invest.'
facts.source: Federal Reserve History, Liberty Bonds

facts.text: In fiscal 2026, net interest took about 19.5 cents of every dollar the government collected in revenue.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Monthly Treasury Statement Table 9 (September 2026)
facts.note: Net Interest $1,051.8B divided by total receipts $5,403.3B = 19.5 percent.

facts.text: Surpluses in the 1920s cut the national debt by more than a third, from $26.0 billion in 1920 to $16.2 billion in 1930.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Historical Debt Outstanding
facts.note: 1920-06-30 = $25.95 billion; 1930-06-30 = $16.19 billion; decline 37.6 percent.

facts.text: The Federal Reserve held $4.78 trillion of Treasury debt in mid-2026, down from a $6.25 trillion peak in early 2022.
facts.source: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis: Federal Debt Held by Federal Reserve Banks
facts.note: FRED FDHBFRBN: 2026 Q2 = 4,780.1 billion; maximum 6,254.966 billion in 2022 Q1.

facts.text: In 1898, Congress let small investors buy part of $400 million in bonds to help fund the Spanish-American War.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service RL31967, The Debt Limit: History and Recent Increases

facts.text: After a $3.2 billion surplus in 1969, the federal budget did not balance again until 1998.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: The debt limit is $41.1 trillion, and outside projections say the debt could reach it in early to mid 2027.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service IF10292, The Debt Limit (updated Sept 21, 2026)

facts.text: Bonds paid for about two-thirds of World War I and taxes the rest: more than $17 billion versus $8.8 billion.
facts.source: Federal Reserve History, Liberty Bonds

facts.text: One year of net interest in fiscal 2026 ($1.05 trillion) exceeded the entire national debt in 1981 ($998 billion).
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Monthly Treasury Statement Table 9 (September 2026)
facts.note: MTS Table 9 net interest $1,051.8B; Historical Debt Outstanding 1981-09-30 = $997.9B.

facts.text: From April 1942, the Fed held Treasury bill rates at 3/8 percent to keep World War II borrowing cheap.
facts.source: Federal Reserve History, The Treasury-Fed Accord

facts.text: World War II War Stamps cost as little as 10 cents, so any citizen could lend Washington a dime.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of U.S. Savings Bonds (timeline)

facts.text: The last two trillions took about five months each: 147 days to reach $39 trillion and 154 days to reach $40 trillion.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny

facts.text: The national debt ended fiscal 1981 at $998 billion and a year later stood at $1.14 trillion, passing $1 trillion.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Historical Debt Outstanding

facts.text: In 1943, the Hollywood Bond Cavalcade sent Lucille Ball, Judy Garland and Mickey Rooney on tour to sell war bonds.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of U.S. Savings Bonds (timeline)

facts.text: As of September 30, 2026, $7.1 trillion of the debt was in Treasury bills, which mature in a year or less.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Monthly Statement of the Public Debt Table 1 (September 2026)
facts.note: MSPD Table 1: Bills = $7,118,145 million. TreasuryDirect: bills have terms from 4 weeks to 52 weeks.

facts.text: The 14th Amendment, ratified July 9, 1868, declared debts incurred to aid the rebellion 'illegal and void.'
facts.source: National Archives, Constitution Amendments 11-27

facts.text: If rates run 1.5 points above CBO's February forecast through 2036, deficits would grow by $6 trillion, CBO estimates.
facts.source: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, on CBO's interest-rate analysis (Oct 8, 2026)

facts.text: By the end of World War II, Savings Bonds made up nearly 18 percent of the total public debt.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: From 1980 to 1990, the national debt more than tripled, from $908 billion to $3.2 trillion.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Historical Debt Outstanding

facts.text: China's Treasury holdings fell to $618 billion in July 2026, less than half the $1.317 trillion peak of November 2013.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury, Treasury International Capital Table 5: Major Foreign Holders of Treasury Securities (July 2026)
facts.note: TIC Table 5: China $618.0B in July 2026. Treasury history file (mfhhis01): peak $1,316.7B in November 2013; 618.0 / 1,316.7 = 47 percent.

facts.text: On October 16, 2013, Congress suspended the debt limit the night before Treasury's borrowing room was expected to run out.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service RL31967, The Debt Limit: History and Recent Increases

facts.text: Only Social Security and Medicare cost more than net interest in fiscal 2026, by Treasury's spending categories.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Monthly Treasury Statement Table 9 (September 2026)
facts.note: MTS Table 9 FY2026: Social Security $1,667B; Medicare $1,073B; Net Interest $1,052B; Health $1,026B; National Defense $965B.

facts.text: The national debt more than doubled in five years, from $1.14 trillion in 1982 to $2.35 trillion in 1987.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Historical Debt Outstanding

facts.text: A March 4, 1951 Treasury-Fed Accord ended the wartime peg that had forced the Fed to keep buying government debt.
facts.source: Federal Reserve History, The Treasury-Fed Accord

facts.text: The debt grew $2.5 trillion in fiscal 2026, more than the entire national debt at the end of fiscal 1987.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Historical Debt Outstanding

facts.text: Surpluses from 1998 to 2001 cut debt held by the public by roughly $600 billion, from about $3.9 trillion to $3.3 trillion.
facts.source: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis: Federal Debt Held by the Public
facts.note: FRED FYGFDPUN: 1998 Q1 = $3.872T; 2001 Q2 = $3.274T (difference $598B). CRS IF10292 confirms debt held by the public declined between 1998 and 2001.

facts.text: On October 5, 2026, the 10-year Treasury yield closed at 5.31 percent, its highest close since 2002.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury, Daily Treasury Par Yield Curve Rates
facts.note: 2026 maximum 10-year par yield = 5.31 on 10/05/2026. Last close at or above 5.31 before that was 5.32 on 05/14/2002; annual maximums 2003 to 2025 were all lower (2007 5.26; 2023 4.98).

facts.text: After the 2013 debt-limit deal, the national debt jumped $328 billion in one day and crossed $17 trillion.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny

facts.text: In 2000, the White House said debt held by the public could be repaid by 2012. In 2026 it tops $32 trillion.
facts.source: White House archives, Statement by the President: National Debt Clock (Sept 7, 2000)
facts.note: White House statement: continued fiscal discipline would keep the country on a path to repay the debt held by the public by 2012. Debt to the Penny, 2026-10-14: debt held by the public = $32.48 trillion.

facts.text: As of October 2026, about $7.8 trillion of the debt is owed to government trust funds and accounts, led by Social Security.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny
facts.note: Debt to the Penny 2026-10-14: intragovernmental holdings $7.846T. Fiscal Data guide: the Social Security Administration is the largest investor in Treasury securities.

facts.text: On August 2, 2011, the day a debt-limit deal was signed, the national debt rose $238 billion in a single day.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny
facts.note: 2011-08-01 = $14.342T; 2011-08-02 = $14.581T; increase $238.3B. CRS RL31967: Budget Control Act signed August 2, 2011.

facts.text: Net interest in fiscal 2026 came to about $7,800 for every U.S. household.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Monthly Treasury Statement Table 9 (September 2026)
facts.note: $1,051.8B divided by 134.79 million households = $7,803.

facts.text: World War II cost about $323 billion, and the Treasury borrowed roughly $211 billion of it.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: Four days after the 2011 debt-limit deal, S&P cut the U.S. from AAA to AA+, the first downgrade of its kind.
facts.source: PBS NewsHour, S&P downgrades US credit rating from AAA for first time (Aug 5, 2011)
facts.note: S&P downgrade August 5, 2011; Budget Control Act signed August 2, 2011 (CRS RL31967).

facts.text: Treasury's daily debt records begin on April 1, 1993, when the national debt stood at $4.23 trillion.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny
facts.note: First Debt to the Penny record: 1993-04-01 = $4,225,873,987,843.44.

facts.text: World War I bond drives used 11,000 donated billboards and streetcar ads in 3,200 cities.
facts.source: Federal Reserve History, Liberty Bonds

facts.text: After the June 3, 2023 debt-limit law, the national debt jumped $359 billion by the next business day, June 5.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny
facts.note: 2023-06-02 = $31.467T; 2023-06-05 = $31.826T; increase $358.6B. Fiscal Responsibility Act (P.L. 118-5) enacted June 3, 2023.

facts.text: Fiscal 2026 ended with spending of $7.40 trillion against revenue of $5.40 trillion, a gap of about 27 cents per dollar spent.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Monthly Treasury Statement Table 9 (September 2026)
facts.note: Outlays $7,395.8B; receipts $5,403.3B; deficit $1,992.5B = 26.9 percent of outlays.

facts.text: In spring 2020, the debt added a trillion dollars in just 28 days, the fastest pace in Treasury's daily data since 1993.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny
facts.note: First record at or above $24T is 2020-04-07; first at or above $25T is 2020-05-05 (28 days). Daily data begin 1993-04-01; no other trillion took fewer than 35 days.

facts.text: CBO projects the federal debt subject to the limit will reach $63.8 trillion by the end of fiscal 2036.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service IF10292, The Debt Limit (updated Sept 21, 2026)

facts.text: From fiscal 2000 to fiscal 2026, the national debt grew about sevenfold, from $5.7 trillion to $40.2 trillion.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Historical Debt Outstanding

facts.text: Congress has changed the debt limit 104 times since World War II, including 22 times since 2001.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service IF10292, The Debt Limit (updated Sept 21, 2026)

facts.text: Total federal debt is about 122 percent of GDP, larger than a full year of U.S. economic output.
facts.source: Peter G. Peterson Foundation, With $40 Trillion in Debt, Is the U.S. Headed for More Credit Downgrades?

facts.text: After the July 2025 law raised the debt limit by $5 trillion, the national debt jumped $366 billion in four days.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny
facts.note: 2025-07-03 = $36.216T; 2025-07-07 = $36.582T; increase $366.4B. CRS IF10292: P.L. 119-21 raised the limit by $5.0 trillion to $41.1 trillion; signed July 4, 2025.

facts.text: Interest costs now run more than triple the roughly $350 billion a year paid from 2018 to 2021.
facts.source: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, FY 2026 deficit estimate (Oct 1, 2026)

facts.text: On November 2, 2015, Congress suspended the debt limit one day before Treasury said it would run out of options.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service RL31967, The Debt Limit: History and Recent Increases
facts.note: CRS RL31967: Secretary Lew said extraordinary measures would be exhausted no later than November 3, 2015; the suspension was signed November 2.
